authoring.note: A sealed storm-drain access set into the Landing End's own ground -- part of the fortress island's own drainage, not the mainland's; whatever is down there is a separate problem from anything under the old town. The cover carries a maintenance code with no scheduled visit against it in some time, and at high tide something moves down there loud enough to hear from the street.

lore.playerFacing: A cast-iron cover, flush with the road, stamped with a maintenance code and not much else. It sits a little proud of true, like it's been lifted and reseated more than once by somebody in a hurry. On a still day, at high tide, you can hear something move underneath it -- not loud, not close, but enough.
lore.gmOnly:
Not connected to episode-c1e1--flood-tunnel (the old-town, mainland drainage chamber -- data/locations/old-landing.json). Kept deliberately separate; do not conflate the two when planning a session. No encounter is written for this site yet. If one ever is, c1e1-flood-tunnel's own Giant Centipede stat reference (data/encounters/c1e1-flood-tunnel.json) and its non-sentient-animal framing (quarantine/ideas/story/bible/species/mitflits.md) are the right starting point rather than inventing a new creature from scratch -- keep whatever's down here equally non-sentient, for the same reason that fight isn't mitflits.

Landing End's own constraints apply: no civilians know this is here, and nothing about it should read as anything but a maintenance problem to anyone who isn't Directorate.

hooks: A candidate on a punishment detail draws the short straw and has to check the cover after a heavy tide -- and finds it's been moved from the inside.
At high tide, on a still night, the sound from underneath is loud enough that somebody eventually has to explain it to a newly posted officer who wasn't warned.
activities: Investigate the cover and whatever's moving beneath it -- if command ever actually authorises going down there.
Stand watch over it at high tide, when the noise is worst, on whatever detail draws the short straw.
Report the maintenance code up the chain and get told, again, that a visit is scheduled -- eventually.
